prize_parts.citation: For developing targeted protein degradation, in which small molecules induce proximity between an E3 ubiquitin ligase and a chosen protein, from heterobifunctional PROTACs to the cereblon-mediated mechanism of molecular glue degraders

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B063 with Crews, Deshaies and Handa. After round 1 the case is firmer on one point. Chabes, Linke and I independently reached the same three names from different starting points, and Linke moved B063 from fourth to first for the same reason I hold it, that the credit divides into a concept strand (Crews and Deshaies, who showed that a bifunctional small molecule can recruit an E3 ligase to a chosen protein) and a mechanism strand (Handa, who identified cereblon as the thalidomide target and so explained molecular glues). I now treat those strands as one idea, induced proximity, expressed in two chemistries. The chemical content is explicit and teachable: ligand and linker design, ternary-complex cooperativity, and a molecular explanation for a drug class that had been used for decades without one. It is reproduced in many independent laboratories and has changed how chemical biologists remove a protein acutely. I rest the case on originality and mechanistic depth, not on the breadth of opening rankings, which I agree with Linke does not by itself prove merit.
statement.case_against: Timing remains the main reservation and I cannot dismiss it. No degrader is approved, so the therapeutic payoff is prospective, and the committee would be honouring a modality on mechanism and early clinical proof-of-concept. My answer to the chair's first question is that I do not regard the absence of an approval as disqualifying, because the Nobel standard here is the chemical discovery and its independent confirmation, and the cereblon mechanism already explains approved thalidomide-class drugs, which gives the glue strand real clinical grounding. I accept that a prize the year after a first approval would be easier to defend. Attribution is the second weakness. Ciulli's VHL ligands made PROTACs drug-like and are not replaceable, Ito shares the cereblon discovery with Handa, and Gray, Sakamoto and Kim also have claims. Any three-person cut is exclusionary, and a citation spanning PROTACs and glues can look like two discoveries joined for convenience.

responses.point: Linke moved B063 to first place because the credit splits into a concept strand and a mechanism strand, and asks whether Deshaies, Ciulli or Ito should displace one of the three, or whether a PROTAC/glue split would be cleaner.
responses.response: I welcome the move and agree with the reasoning. On displacement, I looked again at Ciulli. His VHL ligand work is what made PROTACs a credible drug modality, and I would be uncomfortable calling Deshaies's place secure on chemistry alone. But Deshaies and Crews jointly proposed and demonstrated the PROTAC concept and are inseparable on that strand, and Handa is the only name on the mechanism strand if we keep to three, because Ito's claim, though real, is the same discovery shared. I would not replace any of the three. If the committee wanted a larger cut I would add Ciulli before Ito, but the limit of three people stops that. I do not favour splitting into two parts. A two-part split would use up the three-person limit with at most one or two names each and would present induced proximity as two unrelated achievements, which I think misreads the science.

responses.point: Chabes weighs the breadth of support heavily, asks what clinical milestones would be sufficient to treat the modality as mature, and questions the omission of Ciulli, Gray and Sakamoto.
responses.response: I give breadth of ranking less weight than you do, but I agree it is not noise: all eight of us independently placed B063 on a ballot, which means no member regards it as scientifically weak. On milestones, the evidence I would accept is independent human proof that the target is degraded and that this produces a response, together with a defined mechanism of action, and I think the field already has that. Approval would strengthen the case but should not be a precondition. On omissions, I accept Ciulli, Gray and Sakamoto are real losses. Sakamoto's early PROTAC work with Crews and Deshaies is the most direct claim, but it is the same concept strand and a Crews-Deshaies citation already covers its core. Gray's contribution is largely on the glue and covalent-degrader side, where Handa's mechanism is the foundation. The prize cannot reach everyone, and I would sooner state this openly than pretend the three names settle the history.

responses.point: Sparr prefers ionizable lipid nanoparticles (Cullis, Hope, Madden), arguing it has the strongest impact and the cleanest chemical concept, and asks whether first degrader approval would move B063 ahead.
responses.response: Your lipid self-assembly argument is the best case for B035 I have read, and I agree that its maturity is not in question. My concern is no longer maturity but definition. By your own account in the uncertainties, the committee has to decide who holds the third place, with Madden, Anderson, MacLachlan and Langer all argued for, and whether the achievement is chemistry rather than pharmaceutical technology after the 2023 Medicine prize. A prize whose names and field are both disputed is a larger risk than one whose only open point is clinical timing. I would move B035 to first if the committee settled the Vancouver allocation. On your question, an approval would help B063, but the committee should not have to wait for it. The B063 names are agreed by three members; the B035 names are not agreed even between you and Aqvist, who supports Cullis and Anderson.

responses.point: Aqvist proposes a two-part prize of ionizable lipid nanoparticles (Cullis, Anderson) with base editing (Liu alone), and says degradation has the most chemical novelty but ranks behind them on attribution and clinical maturity.
responses.response: Thank you for moving from prime editing to base editing. I agree it is the better-matured genome-editing candidate and that a Liu-only citation is cleaner than the alternatives for prime editing. I still prefer a single part. First, the pairing puts two achievements that sit next to biology and medicine in one prize, and you note yourself that 2020 and 2023 both lie nearby. Second, your argument against B063 on attribution is weaker than the same argument against your own B035 part, where you name two people from a field of six claimants and leave Hope, Madden and MacLachlan out. Third, base editing is under a decade old and its long-term safety is not established, which is the maturity argument you use against degradation. I agree that if the committee prefers a two-part prize, B035 with B068 is a coherent set, and I keep both as alternatives.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a prize for B063 before the first degrader approval, or consider the cereblon mechanism for approved thalidomide-class drugs a sufficient clinical anchor
Whether Ciulli's VHL ligand work outweighs Deshaies's place if the committee judges the PROTAC strand has more claimants than the three-person limit can hold
Whether the citation for B063 reads as one induced-proximity idea or as two discoveries joined
Whether the B035 attribution can be settled in the committee, and whether lipid nanoparticle delivery is regarded as chemistry rather than pharmaceutical technology
statement.conflict_note: No change. I disclose no personal or institutional tie to the PROTAC, cereblon, lipid nanoparticle or genome-editing groups. My peptide, nanoparticle and biosensor research is not directly connected to any of these candidates. My profile shows postdoctoral mentors Molly Stevens and Freddy Boey, neither of whom appears on a shortlisted ballot. I recommend no recusal for any member.
